name: Management consultant
summary: Management consulting interviews are known for the case interview: you're given a business problem, such as falling profits or whether to enter a new market, and talk through how you'd solve it, with some maths along the way. Firms commonly pair cases with questions on your past experience and leadership, and some add an online problem-solving test, such as McKinsey's Solve, or a written case.
rounds: CV and cover letter screen, often with an online problem-solving test at some firms
First-round interviews: usually one or two cases plus questions on your experience
Final-round interviews with senior consultants or partners: harder cases and deeper questions on your experience
For some firms or offices, a written case or a group exercise
looks_for: Structuring a messy problem into clear parts
Quick, accurate mental maths and sense-checking numbers
Hypothesis-driven thinking: saying what you think and testing it
A clear recommendation and its 'so what' for the client
Leadership, teamwork and impact in your past experience
Calm, clear communication you'd trust in front of a client

questions.text: Tell me about a time you led a team through a difficult situation.
covers: The situation and why it was hard
What you did yourself to move the team forward
The result and what the team said or did afterwards

questions.text: Tell me about a time you persuaded someone more senior to change their mind.
covers: Their view and why they held it
How you built your case: data, timing, allies
What changed, and how you kept the relationship strong

questions.text: What's the achievement you're most proud of, and what exactly was your part in it?
covers: Why it was hard and why it mattered
Your own actions, separated from the team's
A measurable result

questions.text: Tell me about a time you got something wrong under pressure.
covers: A real mistake, owned in the first person
How you noticed and what you did to fix it
What you now do differently

questions.text: A regional coffee chain's profits have fallen for two years while its sales held steady. How would you find out why?
covers: A clear structure: revenue versus costs, then digging into costs since sales held
Questions about rent, staff, ingredient prices, product mix and new stores
A hypothesis, how you'd test it and a recommendation

questions.text: Estimate how many cups of tea are sold in Bengaluru each day.
covers: An approach: population times tea drinkers times cups, or outlets times cups per outlet
Rounded numbers, with each assumption said out loud
A sense-check of the answer against something you know

questions.text: A two-wheeler maker is thinking of launching an electric scooter. What would you want to know before advising them?
covers: The market: demand, growth, customers and competitors
The client's strengths: brand, dealers, technology, costs
The economics and risks: investment, margins, battery supply, regulation

questions.text: A hospital wants to cut patient waiting times without hiring more doctors. How would you approach it?
covers: Mapping the patient journey and measuring where the waits happen
Fixes such as scheduling, triage, moving tasks to other staff, faster test results
How you'd pilot changes and measure them, keeping quality of care safe

questions.text: A product costs 40 to make and sells for 50. If costs rise by 10%, what price keeps the same percentage margin?
covers: Working out today's margin first: 10 on 50, or 20%
The new cost of 44, and the price where 44 is 80% of it: 55
Saying the answer clearly, then what might stop the client raising prices

questions.text: A client's sales are up 20% this year, but profit is down. What are your first three questions?
covers: Have costs grown faster than sales, and which ones
Has the mix shifted to lower-margin products, customers or channels
Discounts, one-off costs or accounting changes

questions.text: How would you size the market for online tutoring for school students in this country?
covers: Choosing a route: students, the share who'd pay, and spend per student per year
Splitting by grade or city type where it changes the numbers
A range rather than one figure, and the assumption that matters most

questions.text: What makes a good structure for a case, and when does a standard framework get in the way?
covers: Parts that don't overlap and together cover the problem
Built for this problem, not recited from memory
Prioritising the branch most likely to explain the answer

questions.text: You've found that a retailer's losses come mostly from two store formats. Give the CEO your recommendation in under a minute.
covers: The answer first, then two or three reasons
The numbers that back it up
The risks and the next steps

questions.text: A client manager disagrees with your findings in front of their boss. What would you do?
covers: Staying calm and asking what they see differently
Going back to the data together, and admitting if they have a point
Following up afterwards so they don't feel ambushed

questions.text: Walk me through your CV.
covers: A short, ordered story, not every line
Two or three moments that show leadership, problem-solving or impact
How it leads to consulting now

questions.text: Why consulting, and why our firm rather than another?
covers: What you want from the work: variety, problem-solving, learning fast
Something specific about the firm: its practices, people you've met, the work it publishes
Why you'd do well in the job, not just why you want it

questions.text: Where do you see yourself in five years, and how does consulting fit into that?
covers: An honest direction, even if it isn't fixed
What you'd learn in consulting that you need for it
Showing you've thought about the job's demands

questions.text: Here's a chart of a client's costs by region over three years. What's the one thing you'd tell the client, and what would you check next?
covers: The headline the chart actually supports, said first
The number behind it, read correctly
One sensible next question or data request

questions.text: A bank wants more young customers to open accounts. Brainstorm the ways it could do that.
covers: A clear split of the ideas (product, price, channels, partnerships)
Ideas that are specific rather than generic
Which two you'd test first, and why

questions.text: Tell me about a time you had to work with data you didn't fully trust.
covers: What made the data doubtful
How you checked it or worked around it
How you told others how sure you were

tips: Practise cases out loud with a partner; reading cases isn't the same as solving one under time pressure.
Build a structure for each case rather than reciting a memorised framework.
Do mental maths every day: percentages, growth rates, large multiplications. Round sensibly and say your assumptions.
When you summarise, lead with the answer, then give the reasons.
Prepare three or four stories (leadership, persuasion, failure, teamwork) with your exact part and results; firms commonly probe them in depth.
Read each firm's own careers pages on how it interviews; some publish example cases to practise with.

Bain publishes case interview preparation with practice cases on its careers site, and McKinsey's careers site describes the personal experience questions it asks; read both firms' own material before paid guides.
